q: What is Azure Container Registry used for?
opts: Storing and managing private container images and artifacts
Running containers and scaling them based on demand
exp: Azure Container Registry is a private registry for storing and managing container images, Helm charts and other OCI artifacts, close to where you deploy them. It doesn't run containers — ACI, Container Apps, AKS or App Service do — and it doesn't load-balance or monitor them.

q: Which CLI command creates a Standard container registry?
opts: az acr create -g RG1 -n myacr --sku Standard
az acr new -g RG1 -n myacr --tier Standard --create
exp: az acr create -n myacr --sku Standard creates a registry. --sku can be Basic, Standard or Premium. The registry name must be globally unique, because it becomes myacr.azurecr.io. The other commands don't exist.

q: Before pushing with docker, how do you authenticate to ACR using your Entra identity?
opts: docker login with your Entra password
exp: az acr login --name myacr uses your current Azure CLI (Entra) sign-in to get a token for the registry and configures Docker with it, so docker push and docker pull work. There's no need for the admin password. az login alone doesn't configure Docker, and az acr credential show reveals the admin credentials.

q: What is the full image name format for pushing to registry myacr?
exp: Images in Azure Container Registry are named after the registry's login server: <registry>.azurecr.io/<repository>:<tag>, for example myacr.azurecr.io/app:v1. Without the login server, Docker assumes Docker Hub.

q: Which ACR SKU is required for private endpoints (Private Link)?
exp: Private endpoints (Private Link) for Azure Container Registry need the Premium SKU, as do geo-replication and other advanced network features. Basic and Standard registries are reachable only over their public endpoint.

q: A CI pipeline needs to push images to ACR. Least-privilege role?
exp: AcrPush lets an identity push images (and also pull them), which is all a CI pipeline needs. AcrPull can only pull, so pushes would fail. Owner and Contributor are far too broad, since they can also delete or reconfigure the registry.

q: Images must rebuild automatically when their base image is updated. Which feature?
opts: ACR Tasks with base image update triggers
ACR webhooks with a geo-replication trigger
exp: ACR Tasks can build images automatically when their base image changes (a base image update trigger), when source code is committed, or on a schedule. That keeps images patched. Geo-replication copies registries across regions, webhooks only notify, and content trust signs images.

q: How do you copy an image from Docker Hub into ACR without pulling it locally?
exp: az acr import copies an image from another registry, such as Docker Hub or another ACR, directly into your registry on the server side, without pulling it to your machine. az acr build builds from source code, and az acr replicate doesn't exist.

q: Why is the ACR admin account discouraged for production?
opts: It's a single shared username and password with full push/pull rights and no per-user auditing
It works only on the Premium SKU and its password can't be regenerated after creation
exp: The admin account is one shared username and password with full push and pull rights to the whole registry. You can't scope it, and you can't tell who used it. Microsoft recommends Entra identities (users, service principals or managed identities with roles such as AcrPull), or repository-scoped tokens, instead.

q: Which CLI command creates a container instance with a public DNS label?
opts: az container create -g RG1 -n web --image mcr.microsoft.com/azuredocs/aci-helloworld --dns-name-label myweb --ports 80
az webapp create -g RG1 -n web --container mcr.microsoft.com/azuredocs/aci-helloworld --public-dns-name myweb --port 80
exp: az container create runs a container instance. --dns-name-label myweb gives it a public name (myweb.<region>.azurecontainer.io) and --ports 80 opens port 80. The other commands don't exist, and az webapp create makes an App Service app instead.

q: Which CLI command shows a running container instance's logs?
exp: az container logs shows what a container in a container instance has written to stdout and stderr. Add --follow to stream it. docker logs only works with your local Docker, and the other commands don't exist.

q: You need an interactive shell inside a running container in ACI. Use:
exp: az container exec runs a command inside a running container, for example /bin/sh to open an interactive shell. ACI doesn't offer SSH, Bastion or a serial console.

q: Container data must persist after the container stops. What do you do?
opts: Mount an Azure Files share as a volume
exp: A container's own file system is lost when the container stops or restarts. To keep data, mount an Azure Files share as a volume; data written there persists. emptyDir and secret volumes are temporary or read-only.

q: How are CPU and memory assigned in ACI?
opts: You request vCPU and memory per container and are billed per second
By choosing a VM size that all containers in the subscription share
exp: In ACI you request CPU and memory for each container (for example --cpu 1 --memory 1.5), and you're billed per second for what you requested while the container group runs. You don't pick a VM size or use an App Service plan, and the resources aren't fixed at 1 vCPU and 1 GB.

q: A container instance must reach a database on a private IP in VNet1 without a public IP. What do you do?
opts: Deploy the container group into a delegated subnet in VNet1
Add a service endpoint for the container instance to VNet1
exp: Deploying the container group into a subnet of VNet1 (the subnet is delegated to Microsoft.ContainerInstance/containerGroups) gives it a private IP, so it can reach the database privately without a public IP. Peering alone doesn't put the container in a network, and service endpoints are for PaaS services.

q: How do you pass a database password to an ACI container so it isn't shown in the portal?
exp: Secure environment variables (--secure-environment-variables) are passed to the container but aren't shown in the container's properties in the portal or CLI. Ordinary environment variables are visible to anyone who can read the container group. Never put secrets in image names or tags.

q: How do you deploy a multi-container group (app plus sidecar) to ACI?
opts: With a YAML file or ARM template defining the container group
With one az container create per container in the same group
exp: A container group with several containers (for example an app plus a sidecar) is defined in one YAML file or ARM/Bicep template and deployed with az container create --file. Running az container create once per container would create separate groups. The portal can't create multi-container groups.

q: How do you scale an ACI deployment?
opts: ACI has no built-in autoscale; deploy more container groups or change resource requests
Create autoscale rules on the container group's CPU metric and set a maximum of 10
exp: ACI has no built-in autoscaling: each container group runs with the CPU and memory you requested. To handle more load, deploy more container groups or redeploy with bigger requests. For automatic scaling, use Azure Container Apps or AKS.

q: In Azure Container Apps, what's the boundary that groups apps sharing a VNet and Log Analytics workspace?
exp: A Container Apps environment is the shared boundary for a group of container apps: they share a virtual network, ingress and logging (a Log Analytics workspace), and can reach each other. A container group is an ACI concept, an App Service plan is for App Service, and a resource group is only for management.

q: In Container Apps, what is a revision?
opts: An immutable snapshot of a container app version
A scaling rule tied to one container app
exp: A revision is an immutable snapshot of a version of a container app. Changing revision-scoped settings, such as the image or environment variables, creates a new revision, and you can run several revisions and split traffic between them. It isn't a backup, lock or scaling rule.

q: Send 20% of traffic to a new version of a container app and 80% to the old one. What do you configure?
opts: Multiple revision mode with traffic splitting (weights)
Two separate environments with a weighted DNS record
exp: In multiple revision mode, a container app can run several revisions at once, and you set traffic weights between them (for example 80% to the old revision and 20% to the new one) for a canary release. You don't need separate environments, Application Gateway or DNS changes.

q: Which Container Apps scale rule type scales on concurrent HTTP requests?
exp: An HTTP scale rule adds or removes Container Apps replicas based on the number of concurrent HTTP requests. Other rule types use KEDA scalers for events (such as queues), or CPU and memory. Schedule and manual settings don't respond to request load.

q: A container app should be reachable only from other apps in the same environment. Which ingress setting?
exp: Internal ingress makes a container app reachable only from inside its Container Apps environment (and the VNet it's connected to), not from the internet. External ingress exposes it publicly, and with no ingress at all, no other app can call it over HTTP.

q: A scheduled nightly batch task should run in Container Apps and then exit. Which resource?
exp: A Container Apps job runs a container to completion and then stops. Jobs can be triggered manually, on a schedule (cron) or by events. A container app with at least one replica would keep running all the time, ACR Tasks build images, and VMSS is far more to manage.

q: Which TWO services can scale containers automatically based on load without you managing Kubernetes?
opts: Azure App Service (Web App for Containers) with autoscale
exp: Azure Container Apps scales automatically (including to zero) with HTTP and KEDA rules, and App Service (Web App for Containers) scales out with autoscale rules, without you managing Kubernetes. ACI has no autoscaling, and ACR only stores images.

q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: Container Apps can scale to zero replicas
exp: Container Apps can scale down to zero replicas and supports Dapr for microservices. ACI can run Windows containers. Geo-replication in Azure Container Registry is only available in the Premium tier, not Basic.

q: Which App Service tier is intended for free development and testing, with shared infrastructure and no custom domains?
exp: The Free (F1) tier runs apps on shared infrastructure at no cost, for development and testing. It has quotas and no custom domains, scaling or SLA. Standard, Premium and Isolated are paid production tiers.

q: Which tier is the lowest that supports custom domains with SSL bindings and dedicated compute?
exp: Basic is the lowest tier with dedicated compute instances, custom domains and TLS/SSL bindings, though scaling is manual only and limited. Free and Shared run on shared infrastructure and can't use custom domains with TLS. Standard adds autoscale and slots, but isn't the minimum.

q: An app needs full network isolation in a single-tenant environment inside your VNet with very high scale. Which tier?
opts: Premium v3 with regional VNet integration
exp: The Isolated v2 tier runs in an App Service Environment v3, a single-tenant deployment inside your own virtual network. That gives full network isolation and very high scale. Premium v3, Standard and Basic run on shared multi-tenant infrastructure, even though they can integrate with VNets.

q: Three web apps run in one App Service plan with 2 instances. How many instances does each app run on?
opts: 2 — every app runs on all instances of the plan
exp: Every app in an App Service plan runs on all of the plan's instances. With 2 instances, each of the three apps runs on both. You pay for the plan's instances, not per app. Scaling the plan affects every app in it.

q: Can you move a web app to an App Service plan in a different region?
opts: No — the plan must be in the same resource group and region
Yes — but only when both plans are in the Premium tier
exp: An app can only move to another App Service plan in the same resource group and region (the same 'webspace'). To run it in another region, create a new app in a plan there and redeploy the code (or clone the app). Tier and operating system don't change this.

q: What's the maximum instance count of a Standard App Service plan?
exp: A Standard App Service plan can scale out to at most 10 instances. Basic allows up to 3, Premium v3 up to 30, and Isolated up to 100 — so if you need more than 10, move to a higher tier.

q: An app should scale out instantly based on HTTP traffic, without writing autoscale rules (Premium v2/v3). Which feature?
exp: Automatic scaling, available on Premium v2 and v3, lets App Service add and remove instances based on HTTP traffic, with no autoscale rules for you to write. It reacts quickly and keeps instances warm. Manual and scheduled scaling need settings from you, and slots are for deployment.

q: Which CLI command creates a web app in an existing plan?
opts: az webapp create -g RG1 -p plan1 -n myapp123 --runtime "DOTNETCORE:8.0"
az appservice create -g RG1 -p plan1 -n myapp123 --stack "DOTNETCORE:8.0"
exp: az webapp create creates a web app in an existing App Service plan (-p) with a globally unique name (-n) and a runtime such as "DOTNETCORE:8.0". The name becomes <name>.azurewebsites.net. The other commands don't exist.

q: Which CLI command creates a Linux App Service plan at the S1 tier?
opts: az appservice plan create -g RG1 -n plan1 --sku S1 --is-linux
az appservice create -g RG1 -n plan1 --tier S1 --os linux --new-plan
exp: az appservice plan create creates an App Service plan. --sku S1 sets the Standard tier and --is-linux makes it a Linux plan, which Linux web apps need. The other commands don't exist.

q: An app stores its database connection string. Where should non-secret settings and secret references go?
exp: App settings and connection strings are exposed to the app as environment variables, so configuration stays out of the code. For secrets, use a Key Vault reference in the setting (@Microsoft.KeyVault(...)), so the secret stays in Key Vault. Hard-coding settings is insecure, and tags and the plan aren't for configuration.

q: A Key Vault reference in App Service settings fails to resolve. What's the most common missing piece?
opts: The app's managed identity lacks permission on the vault
The vault must be in a different region from the app
exp: A Key Vault reference only works if the app's managed identity can read the secret: a role such as Key Vault Secrets User (with the RBAC model) or a Get secret access policy. Without it, the setting fails to resolve. Any tier above Free works, the vault can be in any region, and slots don't matter.

q: Continuous WebJobs stop running when there's no traffic. Which setting fixes this?
exp: Without Always On, App Service unloads an idle app after about 20 minutes with no requests, which also stops continuous WebJobs. Always On keeps the app loaded (available from Basic). ARR affinity, HTTP/2 and Auto heal don't keep the app running.

q: A stateless app behind multiple instances has unbalanced load because users stick to one instance. What do you disable?
exp: ARR affinity (on by default) sets a cookie that sends each user back to the same instance. A stateless app doesn't need that, and it can leave some instances overloaded. Turning ARR affinity off lets the load balancer spread requests evenly. The other settings don't affect distribution.

q: App Service should stop routing traffic to an instance that fails a /health endpoint check. Which feature?
exp: Health check pings a path you choose, such as /health, on every instance. An instance that keeps failing is taken out of the load balancer rotation (and replaced if it stays unhealthy). Auto heal restarts on conditions you set, access restrictions filter callers, and logging only records events.

q: How many deployment slots (including production) does the Standard tier allow?
exp: The Standard tier allows 5 deployment slots, counting production, and Premium allows 20. Free, Shared and Basic don't support slots, so if you need a staging slot, you need at least Standard.

q: Which CLI command swaps the staging slot with production?
opts: az webapp deployment slot swap -g RG1 -n myapp --slot staging --target-slot production
az webapp swap -g RG1 -n myapp --from-slot staging --to-slot production --preview
exp: az webapp deployment slot swap --slot staging --target-slot production swaps the staging slot into production (warming it up first). The other commands don't exist.

q: You want 10% of production users to hit the staging slot for testing. Which feature?
exp: Testing in production (traffic routing) sends a percentage of production traffic, such as 10%, to another slot, so real users try the new version while the rest stay on production. Swap with preview pauses a swap rather than splitting traffic, and access restrictions and ARR affinity don't route users between slots.

q: Every time code is pushed to staging, it must automatically swap to production after warm-up. Which feature?
exp: With auto swap enabled on the staging slot, every deployment to staging is warmed up and then automatically swapped into production, with no manual step. Traffic routing splits users between slots, swap with preview needs you to complete it, and clone app copies an app.

q: To map the apex domain contoso.com (no www) to an App Service app, which DNS records are used?
opts: An A record with the app's IP, plus a TXT record asuid for verification
A CNAME at the apex, plus an MX record for verification
exp: CNAME records aren't allowed at a zone's apex (contoso.com), so map it with an A record pointing to the app's inbound IP address, plus a TXT record named asuid with the app's verification ID to prove you own the domain. MX is for email and NS for delegation.

q: All HTTP requests to an app must be redirected to HTTPS. Which setting?
exp: HTTPS Only = On makes App Service redirect every HTTP request to HTTPS. The minimum TLS version controls which TLS versions are accepted (and 1.0 would weaken security), client certificates are for mutual TLS, and Always On keeps the app loaded.

q: A wildcard certificate (*.contoso.com) must secure several App Service apps. What should you use?
opts: Import the certificate (from Key Vault or a PFX upload)
A free App Service managed certificate for each app
A Let's Encrypt cert via the portal
exp: Free App Service managed certificates don't support wildcard domains. To secure *.contoso.com across several apps, import the wildcard certificate — from Key Vault, a PFX upload or an App Service certificate — and bind it to each app. Client certificates are for authenticating callers, not for the site.

q: An internal web app must be reachable ONLY from your VNet and on-premises (over VPN), with no public exposure. Which feature?
opts: A private endpoint for the app (and disabling public access)
Access restrictions on the app that allow any source address
exp: A private endpoint gives the app a private IP in your VNet, so it's reachable from the VNet and from on-premises over VPN. Disabling public network access then blocks the internet. VNet integration is only for outbound calls, Hybrid Connections reach on-premises hosts, and allowing Any keeps the app public.

q: Where are custom (scheduled) App Service backups stored?
opts: In a storage account container you choose
In a Recovery Services vault with GRS
exp: Custom (scheduled or on-demand) App Service backups are written as ZIP and XML files to a storage account container that you choose. Automatic backups are stored by the platform itself. App Service backups don't use Recovery Services vaults or Key Vault.

ctx: App1 runs on a Basic B1 Linux plan. Requirements: staging slot, CPU-based autoscale, a free TLS certificate for www.contoso.com, and outbound access to a VM's private IP.
q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: B1 supports a staging deployment slot
A free managed certificate can be used for www.contoso.com on B1
Regional VNet integration is available on B1
exp: Basic B1 doesn't support deployment slots or rule-based autoscale — both need Standard or higher. A free managed certificate does work for www.contoso.com on B1, and regional VNet integration is available on Basic. So B1 meets the TLS and network requirements, but not staging or autoscale.

q: You are designing encryption for new VMs that must run past 2028. Temp disks and caches must be encrypted too. Which option does Microsoft recommend?
opts: Azure Disk Encryption with a key encryption key
Server-side encryption with platform-managed keys only
Infrastructure encryption on a storage account
exp: Encryption at host covers temp disks, caches and the data flow to storage, and Microsoft recommends it for new VMs. Azure Disk Encryption is scheduled for retirement on 15 September 2028, after which encrypted disks fail to unlock on reboot. Server-side encryption alone doesn't cover temp disks or caches.

q: VM1 (Windows) uses Azure Disk Encryption. How do you move it to encryption at host?
opts: Turn on encryption at host while ADE is still enabled
Run az vm encryption migrate and restart the VM
Change the key vault's access setting to EncryptionAtHost
Disable ADE, create new disks by upload, then create a new VM
exp: There's no in-place conversion. You disable ADE and confirm the disks are fully decrypted, create new managed disks with the upload method (snapshots and disk copies keep the ADE flag), and create a new VM from them with encryption at host on. The VM has downtime during the move.

q: Which TWO are advantages of encryption at host over Azure Disk Encryption?
opts: It doesn't use the VM's CPU
It encrypts disks only after the VM is deleted
It works with custom Linux images
It removes the need for managed disks
exp: Encryption at host runs on the host, so it doesn't use the VM's CPU, and it works with custom images. Azure Disk Encryption runs inside the guest, uses the VM's CPU and doesn't support custom Linux images. Both protect the disks while the VM is in use.

q: You want a Bicep file for the resources that already exist in RG1. Put the steps in order.
items: Review and fix the generated Bicep file
Run az group export --name RG1 > main.json
Deploy the Bicep file with az deployment group create
exp: First export the resource group to an ARM JSON template, then decompile that JSON to Bicep. Decompiling is a best-effort conversion with no guaranteed mapping, so review and fix the file before you deploy it.

q: You run az bicep decompile on a large ARM template. Which statement is true about the result?
opts: It is always identical to what a person would write
It is deployed to Azure as soon as it has been created
It is a best-effort conversion that you should review
It is stored in the template's own resource group
exp: Decompile tries to convert ARM JSON to Bicep, but there's no guaranteed mapping, so you may need to fix warnings or errors and tidy names. It writes a .bicep file to the same folder as the JSON. It doesn't deploy anything to Azure.

q: A running container group in Azure Container Instances needs more memory. What must you do?
opts: Delete the container group and deploy it again with the new value
Change the memory in the portal while the group keeps running
Add an autoscale rule that uses the group's memory metric
Restart the group with the --memory parameter in Azure CLI
exp: CPU, memory and GPU requests of a container group can't be updated in place. You delete the group and deploy it again with the new values. A restart keeps the old values, and Container Instances has no autoscale rules.

q: A container group has two containers. One requests 1 CPU and 1.5 GB, and the other requests 1 CPU and 2 GB. How much does Azure allocate to the group?
exp: A container group gets the sum of the requests of all its containers: 1 + 1 = 2 CPU and 1.5 + 2 = 3.5 GB of memory. The containers share the group's resources, and you pay for what the group was allocated.

q: You create a container app with ingress enabled and define no scale rule. What are the default scale settings?
exp: When you define no rule, Container Apps uses an HTTP scale rule with a minimum of 0 and a maximum of 10 replicas. With a minimum of 0, the app can scale to zero when there's no traffic, and you pay no usage charges while it's at zero.

q: Which TWO statements about scaling in Azure Container Apps are true?
opts: The maximum number of replicas can be set up to 1,000
A container app scales vertically when it runs out of memory
The default minimum number of replicas is 0
Scale rules can only use HTTP requests
exp: Minimum replicas default to 0 and maximum replicas default to 10, and the maximum can be raised to 1,000. Container Apps scales horizontally by adding replicas: vertical scaling isn't supported. Rules can use HTTP, TCP or custom (KEDA-based) triggers such as queue length or CPU.

q: Which pricing tier is the lowest that supports App Service backups?
exp: App Service backups, both automatic and custom, need the Basic, Standard, Premium or Isolated tier, so Basic is the lowest. In Basic you can back up only the production slot. Free and Shared don't support backups.

q: You need App Service backups that you can download and keep for longer than 30 days. What do you use?
opts: Automatic backups with a longer retention
Custom backups to a storage account
exp: Custom backups are written to a storage account that you choose, so you can download them and keep them for as long as you like. Automatic backups run hourly and are kept for 30 days: the retention can't be changed and they can't be downloaded. Recovery Services vaults don't back up App Service apps.

q: Answer Yes or No about App Service backups:
stmts: Automatic backups need a storage account
Automatic backups are kept for 30 days
A custom backup can be up to 10 GB
Custom backups can run at most 12 times a day
exp: Automatic backups need no storage account and no setup, run hourly, and are kept for 30 days. Custom backups need a storage account, can be up to 10 GB each, and can run every 2 hours at most, which gives up to 12 backups a day.
